Most variations move H0H_{0} slightly upward, by +0.2​σbase+0.2\,\sigma_{\rm base} on average, so that our baseline lies at the lower end of the range spanned by the alternative choices.

Prior on Ωm\Omega_{\rm m}.

Replacing the supernova constraint by a flat prior on Ωm∈[0.05,0.5]\Omega_{\rm m}\in[0.05,0.5] isolates how much of the inference is carried by the external data set rather than by the lenses. Since time-delay cosmography constrains H0H_{0} far better than it constrains Ωm\Omega_{\rm m}, this variation mainly widens the H0H_{0} uncertainty from 3.3% to 4.9%, instead of displacing the median value. Replacing the Ωm\Omega_{\rm m} prior from DES-Dovekie with the DESI BAO distances changes H0H_{0} by +0.6 km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} (+0.3​σbase+0.3\,\sigma_{\rm base}) with similar precision.

External lens samples.

The baseline uses the time-delay lenses alone. Adding the SLACS lenses with KCWI kinematics, the SL2S lenses, and both together, relies on the assumption that the mass profiles of the lens population are shared across samples. In turn, the combined analysis allows the external lenses to constrain λint\lambda_{\rm int} and the anisotropy without contributing any time delay of their own. This is a more precise result at the cost of an additional assumption.

Priors on the population scatter.

In the baseline, the width of some population distribution, i.e., the scatter of λint\lambda_{\rm int}, and of the anisotropy parameter carries a scale-invariant 1/σ1/\sigma (log-uniform) prior. The variation replaces these with uniform priors on the population scatter parameters, i.e. σ⁡(λint)∈[0.001−0.5]\sigma(\lambda_{\rm int})\in[0.001-0.5] and σ⁡(σt/σr)∈[0.03−1]\sigma(\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r})\in[0.03-1]). The two choices differ in how much weight is given to small scatter, so this variation probes the sensitivity of the population widths to a prior choice that is only weakly informed by the data. The effect on H0H_{0} is negligible (−0.1​σbase-0.1\,\sigma_{\rm base}, same precision).

Flattening of the mass model.

The axisymmetric kinematic model requires the observed axis ratio qobsq_{\rm obs}, which determines the inclination and thus the projection of the dynamical model. In our baseline analysis, we use the axis ratio of the total mass distribution inferred from the lens model, while the variation uses the axis ratio of the lens light. These two quantities differ systematically, with the mass generally being rounder than the light distribution (with the exception of RX J1131−-1231 and WGD 2038−-4008). We consider the mass axis ratio qmq_{\rm m} to be a more appropriate tracer of the potential shape, as it accounts for both baryonic and dark matter. However, the ellipticity-shear degeneracy can bias qmq_{\rm m} in systems with strong external shear. We therefore test qlightq_{\rm light} as an alternative choice and find that it has only a minor impact on our results, shifting H0H_{0} by +0.2​σbase+0.2\,\sigma_{\rm base}.

Informative priors on the intrinsic axis ratio and anisotropies.

Two population parameters are only weakly constrained by the lensing and kinematic data themselves: the mean intrinsic axis ratio ⟨qint⟩\langle q_{\rm int}\rangle and the mean anisotropy ⟨σt/σr⟩\langle\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r}\rangle. The baseline samples both, together with their population widths. For our three variations, we instead fix them to an external prior qint=0.73±0.08q_{\rm int}=0.73\pm 0.08 and σt/σr=1.00±0.07\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r}=1.00\pm 0.07, taken from the slow rotators of the SDSS-IV MaNGA sample [145]. We test these two priors separately and both at once. Each replaces a sampled mean and scatter by a fixed distribution, so the variation measures how much of the inference rests on the internal calibration of these parameters and how much external information would change it. The prior on qintq_{\rm int} has no effect on H0H_{0}. The anisotropy prior instead shifts H0H_{0} by +0.5​σbase+0.5\,\sigma_{\rm base}. This is the expected consequence of the mass–anisotropy degeneracy: the prior centered on isotropic orbits raises λint,0\lambda_{\rm int,0} from 0.936 to 0.954, and H0H_{0} by the same fraction. The precision on H0H_{0} improves only marginally, to 3.1%.

Cylindrically aligned JAM modeling.

In general, the velocity ellipsoid in early-type galaxies is expected to be spherically aligned [90, see discussion in Sec. 2.1 of]. However, evidence shows that in fast rotators the velocity ellipsoid flattening varies with polar angle in such a way that the overall flattening is approximately cylindrically aligned [174, Fig. 2]. In our sample, 9/11 time-delay deflectors are slow rotators for which the cylindrical alignment is not expected to be the best choice. However, assuming a cylindrical alignment represents a useful extreme assumption to test as a worst-case scenario. In practice, the cylindrical alignment is implemented by using the spherical alignment with the angular variation of Cappellari [90, Eq. 37]. The anisotropy is then parameterized by σz/σR\sigma_{z}/\sigma_{R} rather than by σt/σr\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r}. In this variant, we adopt a uniform prior on ⟨σz/σR⟩∈[0.7,1]\langle\sigma_{z}/\sigma_{R}\rangle\in[0.7,1] and a log-uniform prior on σ⁡(σz/σR)\sigma(\sigma_{z}/\sigma_{R}) identical to the spherically aligned case. This is the largest shift among our variations, +0.7​σbase+0.7\,\sigma_{\rm base} (λint,0\lambda_{\rm int,0} rising from 0.936 to 0.963), which remains well within the statistical uncertainty.

Kinematic bin masking.

As an alternative to our baseline analysis, which does not apply any masking to the kinematic data except in cases of an obvious failure of the kinematic fit, we apply here three different strategies to restrict which bins of the resolved kinematic maps enter the likelihood, each targeting a potential failure mode of our kinematic extraction pipeline:

  • •

    maximum radius: bins beyond a projected radius of 0.8 θE\theta_{\rm E}, are dropped. These are the bins where the surface brightness of the lens galaxy is the lowest and where the light from the quasar and its host galaxy could contaminate the spectrum and potentially affect the velocity dispersion measurement. This choice masks 17 out of the 229 kinematic bins of the TDCOSMO-2026 sample (7%).

  • •

    maximum error: bins whose velocity dispersion is measured with an uncertainty above a 30 km​s−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}} are dropped. This indicates a poorly constrained pPXF fit, which might potentially be inaccurate. This removes 28 kinematic bins out of the TDCOSMO-2026 sample (12%).

  • •

    sigma clipping: a smooth polynomial trend in log10⁡r\log_{10}r is fitted to the map and bins departing from it by more than 3​σ3\sigma of their own uncertainty are dropped. This removes only 4 out of the 229 kinematic bins (2%).

We note that the “maximum radius” and “maximum error” often remove the same low-SNR outer bins, hence explaining the similarity of the +0.6σbase\sigma_{\rm base} and +0.3σbase\sigma_{\rm base} shifts on H0H_{0} that those two runs yield. Each mask changes the number of constraints, but it also modifies the radial leverage on the anisotropy. Removing some of the outer bins tends to reduce the scatter on the anisotropy parameter σt/σr\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r}, resulting in slightly tighter constraints on its mean ⟨σt/σr⟩\langle\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r}\rangle and in a small shift on H0H_{0}.

VIII Comparison with the literature

In this section, we compare our results with the ones obtained previously by the TDCOSMO collaboration in Sections VIII.1, before comparing them with other H0H_{0} measurements from time-delay cosmography in Sections VIII.2. A comparison with independent probes in the context of the Hubble tension is presented in a companion letter (TDCOSMO-2026-PRL).

VIII.1 Comparison with TDCOSMO-2025

Figure 13 places our results in the sequence of H0H_{0} measurements by the TDCOSMO collaboration and its predecessor H0LiCOW. The most visible change with respect to TDCOSMO-2025 is the precision. For the TDCOSMO sample combined with supernovae, the uncertainty decreases from 5.0% (H0=71.6−3.3+3.9H_{0}=71.6^{+3.9}_{-3.3}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}, with Pantheon+) to 3.3% (H0=71.1−2.3+2.4H_{0}=71.1^{+2.4}_{-2.3}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}, with DES-Dovekie), and with the addition of the SLACS and SL2S lenses from 4.6% (74.3−3.7+3.174.3^{+3.1}_{-3.7}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}) to 3.0% (71.3−2.1+2.271.3^{+2.2}_{-2.1}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}), a reduction of about 35% in both cases. This gain results from the larger sample, the new high-quality kinematic data and several methodological improvements. Our most precise result, which combines TDCOSMO-2026, SLACS and SL2S with DESI BAO, H0=72.2−2.2+2.2H_{0}=72.2^{+2.2}_{-2.2}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} (3.0%), approaches the precision of the H0LiCOW (73.3−1.8+1.773.3^{+1.7}_{-1.8}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}, 2.4%) and TDCOSMO-1 power-law (74.2±1.674.2\pm 1.6km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}, 2.2%) measurements. Those results, however, relied on an assumption about the radial mass profile that is equivalent to fixing λint=1\lambda_{\rm int}=1 in the present analysis. TDCOSMO-4 relaxed this assumption on almost the same data, and the uncertainty grew from 2.2% to 7.9% (H0=74.5−6.1+5.6H_{0}=74.5^{+5.6}_{-6.1}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}), because the single-aperture velocity dispersions available at the time could not constrain the internal MST at a competitive level. TDCOSMO-2025 brought this uncertainty back to 5% with much better kinematic data. With the present work, a measurement that makes minimal assumptions on the radial mass profile reaches 3%. This precision is close to what was previously obtained under much more assertive assumptions.

Our central value is fully consistent with that of TDCOSMO-2025. For the TDCOSMO-2026 sample with supernovae, it moves by only 0.5km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}, about 0.15​σ0.15\sigma. The TDCOSMO-2025 baseline used a single-aperture velocity dispersion for seven of its eight lenses, plus 6 and 8 radial bins from JWST/NIRSpec and Keck/KCWI for RX J1131−-1231. These are now replaced by 227 kinematic bins for the nine lenses with spatially resolved kinematics from several instruments, plus aperture measurements for DES J0408−-5354 and WGD 2038−-4008. Interestingly, this extra information does not translate into a much tighter population mean of the internal MST: we find λint=0.94−0.05+0.05\lambda_{\rm int}=0.94^{+0.05}_{-0.05}, compared with λint=0.97−0.05+0.06\lambda_{\rm int}=0.97^{+0.06}_{-0.05} in TDCOSMO-2025, i.e. a precision of 5.3% instead of 5.5%. The gain in H0H_{0} instead comes from the resolved kinematics constraining the MST of each time-delay lens individually, which loosens the coupling between H0H_{0} and the population mean. Better kinematic data informs λint\lambda_{\rm int} for individual lenses, decreasing the relative weight of the population prior in the inference.

The population mean does not tighten further because the data now are good enough to detect intrinsic scatter in λint\lambda_{\rm int} among the time-delay lenses. This scatter was undetected in TDCOSMO-2025, where we found σ⁡(λint)=0.045−0.040+0.066\sigma(\lambda_{\rm int})=0.045^{+0.066}_{-0.040}, consistent with zero. It is now σ⁡(λint)=0.093−0.026+0.038\sigma(\lambda_{\rm int})=0.093^{+0.038}_{-0.026}, statistically consistent with the previous value, but significantly non-zero. This sets a floor on how well the population mean can be determined from only eleven lenses within the current hierarchical analysis. When the external lenses are included, the data prefer a somewhat larger scatter, σ⁡(λint)=0.131−0.022+0.029\sigma(\lambda_{\rm int})=0.131^{+0.029}_{-0.022}. The same trend was present in TDCOSMO-2025, where TDCOSMO+SLACS+SL2S gave σ⁡(λint)=0.127−0.028+0.039\sigma(\lambda_{\rm int})=0.127^{+0.039}_{-0.028}, consistent with the value found by Knabel et al. [88] for the SLACS sample alone. It may indicate that the SLACS deflectors differ slightly from the time-delay deflectors [88], which would challenge the assumption that the two samples are drawn from the same population. In TDCOSMO-2025, it was hypothesized that the scatter partly absorbed the limitations in the modeling of the SLACS kinematics, which were modeled with spherical JAM. We now use axisymmetric JAM and still observe a similar scatter. This might be an indication that the measured scatter is indeed the true intrinsic scatter of the population. Fitting independent λint\lambda_{\rm int} for each lens, rather than using it as a population parameter, may be necessary to reduce the scatter.

The population-level stellar anisotropy, in contrast, remains only weakly constrained. The mean of σt/σr\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r} is 0.987−0.073+0.0820.987^{+0.082}_{-0.073} for the TDCOSMO-2026 sample, compared with 1.023−0.092+0.0691.023^{+0.069}_{-0.092} in TDCOSMO-2025. Both are largely set by the 𝒰⁡(0.87,1.12)\mathcal{U}(0.87,1.12) prior. Adding the SLACS and SL2S posterior shifts the mean slightly toward radial orbits, 0.928−0.044+0.1000.928^{+0.100}_{-0.044}, without narrowing it significantly.

Interestingly, the TDCOSMO-2026 sample alone shows a mild preference for a negative slope of the MST parameter with the ratio of effective to Einstein radius, αλ=−0.038−0.088+0.082\alpha_{\lambda}=-0.038^{+0.082}_{-0.088}, whereas TDCOSMO-2025 found αλ=−0.003−0.051+0.052\alpha_{\lambda}=-0.003^{+0.052}_{-0.051}. As can be seen in Fig. 6, αλ\alpha_{\lambda} is anti-correlated with the mean λint\lambda_{\rm int}, so the low value of λint\lambda_{\rm int} and the negative αλ\alpha_{\lambda} are partly two expressions of the same feature of the data. Adding the 15 SLACS and SL2S lenses, which contribute excellent spatially resolved kinematics, removes the trend completely, αλ=0.016−0.056+0.051,\alpha_{\lambda}=0.016^{+0.051}_{-0.056}, and λint=0.993−0.041+0.042\lambda_{\rm int}=0.993^{+0.042}_{-0.041}. This is remarkably consistent with no departure from a power law. A larger sample of time-delay lenses with resolved kinematics will show whether the time-delay deflectors differ from the SLACS and SL2S deflectors, or whether this is a statistical fluctuation of the present sample.

These results also explain the comparison with the earlier assertive measurements. The TDCOSMO-2026 time-delay lenses deviate, on average, from a pure power law by about 1​σ1\sigma, with λint\lambda_{\rm int} between 0.935 and 0.942 depending on the prior on Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}. This deviation is not statistically significant and accounts for most of the shift with respect to the power-law result of TDCOSMO-1. With the same uniform prior on Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}, we find H0=70.6−3.1+3.9H_{0}=70.6^{+3.9}_{-3.1}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}, 0.9​σ0.9\sigma below TDCOSMO-1. Since H0∝λintH_{0}\propto\lambda_{\rm int} to first order, rescaling our value to λint=1\lambda_{\rm int}=1 gives ≈75.5\approx 75.5km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}}, in agreement with TDCOSMO-1. The trend disappears once the SLACS and SL2S lenses are included: the population mean is then λint=1.002−0.046+0.050\lambda_{\rm int}=1.002^{+0.050}_{-0.046} (uniform Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}), indistinguishable from a power law, and H0=72.1−3.4+4.1H_{0}=72.1^{+4.1}_{-3.4}km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} agrees with TDCOSMO-1 within 0.5​σ0.5\sigma. The consistency is very re-assuring considering that many things have changed since TDCOSMO-1: the sample has expanded, all the kinematic data are new, external convergences are new and NIRCam-based models have replaced older models for three systems.

VIII.2 Comparison with other works

We limit this section to a comparison with other time-delay cosmography estimates, referring to the companion Letter for a more general overview of the Hubble tension.

The main recent development in time-delay cosmography has been the accelerated pace of discovery and exploitation of multiply-imaged supernovae. Four such measurements have been published to date: supernova Refsdal [33, 40]; supernova H0pe [22]; supernova Encore [32, 175]; and supernova Winny [176, 177, 178]. The first three are lensed by a cluster-scale deflector, the last one by a galaxy-scale deflector. The four measurements have precision ranging from ∼\sim6–10%, and they are all in statistical agreement with the TDCOSMO-2026 result. This is encouraging, considering that the potential sources of systematics are very different: galaxy-scale deflectors vs cluster-scale deflectors; time delay measurements in quasars vs supernovae light curves. As the number of supernovae with measured time delays increases, it will be beneficial to carry out a hierarchical analysis of the results to infer a combined estimate accounting for correlated uncertainties. This will provide a very important independent way to measure H0H_{0}.

When more supernovae lensed by galaxies are available, one can imagine carrying out a very similar analysis to the one presented here, fully accounting for the mass-sheet degeneracy. This will yield yet another important test of systematics.

There are also efforts under way to use quasars lensed by clusters to infer H0H_{0} [20, e.g.,]. Those are promising but have not yet reached the precision needed to put our results through a stringent test.

IX Systematics

In this section, we discuss residual systematic errors and our most recent efforts to quantify and mitigate them (Section IX.1). We also briefly revisit the issue of potential selection effects (Section IX.2). These sections were written prior to unblinding, except for the few words presenting unblinded results. As the statistical precision improves, we are continuing to investigate systematic errors, building upon previous work. We focus here on the more recent work on the topic, referring to TDCOSMO-2025 for a discussion of the pre-2025 work.

IX.1 Model assumptions

The main advances in understanding, mitigating, and correcting potential systematics errors since the 2025 milestone are:

  • •

    Uncertainties on the lens models: Several studies have shown that the modeled Fermat potential differences are robust to the choice of lens modeling code and data. Williams et al. [39] modeled the lens WFI 2033−-4723 based on JWST-NIRCam data and using lenstronomy. They found Fermat potential differences that are more precise and consistent within the errors of the estimates based on HST data and the glee code presented by Rusu et al. [51]. The same data were analyzed by an independent team [179] with the independent lensing code Herculens [180]. They found consistent results and comparable uncertainties. Galan et al. [84] analyzed the lens system J1537−-3010 using the same data and two independent codes led by the two lead authors (glee and lenstronomy) and found overall agreement, although the lenstronomy one better fit the data with a more physical model. Williams et al. [85] modeled with lenstronomy three quads that are part of the TDCOSMO-2026 sample combining JWST-NIRCam imaging, JWST-NIRSpec spectroscopy, and new estimates of the external convergence. They compared their results with the previous analysis based on HST imaging, ground-based spectroscopy, and older estimates of κext\kappa_{\rm ext}, finding consistent results and reduced scatter.

  • •

    A central supermassive black hole could affect the interpretation of the stellar velocity dispersion at the JWST-NIRSpec angular resolution [104]. This is now accounted for in our most recent dynamical models. For the systems for which a black hole has been included, we find that it makes no significant difference given the current data [30, see, e.g.,].

  • •

    Departures from spherical symmetry in dynamical models: we have replaced the correction to spherical models [61], with axisymmetric models. Impacts of potential triaxiality are below the 1% level on average [61].

  • •

    Parameterization of the orbital anisotropy: Verma and Minor [75] show using cosmological numerical simulations that the assumption of constant anisotropy adopted in this paper yields unbiased measurements of the H0H_{0}.

In summary, the work done in the past year strengthens the conclusions of TDCOSMO-2025 that the model assumption uncertainties are smaller than the statistical uncertainties associated with our measurement of H0H_{0}, and are uncorrelated. Therefore, they are subdominant in our error budget, and can be neglected for now.

As the statistical uncertainties continue to improve, we will extend this investigation to ensure that systematic errors remain subdominant. This implies updating some of our analysis techniques to explicitly capture additional model degeneracies [147] and establish a detailed error budget per source of uncertainties, either in a data-driven way or based on controlled simulations.

IX.2 Selection effects

As discussed extensively in TDCOSMO-2025, selection effects could potentially bias our result in combination with external datasets.

One potential source of bias is informative priors on population-level hyperparameters taken from external samples. To avoid this potential source of bias we have adopted non-informative priors on the distribution of intrinsic flattening in 3D, rather than relying on the much better characterized distribution estimated from much larger samples of non-lens galaxies [145]. This comes at the cost of two additional population parameters, ⟨qint⟩\langle q_{\rm int}\rangle and σ⁡(qint)\sigma(q_{\rm int}), which need to be constrained by the data of our 11 time-delay lenses. We show in Section VII that adopting a prior from the MaNGA sample would only improve our precision from 3.3% to 3.2%, with no change in the central value of H0H_{0}.

Another potential source of bias is the combination with external samples of non-time-delay lenses. If, for example, the properties of the SLACS and SL2S sample were intrinsically different than those of the time-delay lenses, the inference of λint\lambda_{\rm int} and therefore of H0H_{0} could be biased. It is for this reason that our primary result is that based exclusively on the time-delay lenses, and we report the one in combination as an extension of this work. Reassuringly, the results with and without the external samples are in excellent statistical agreement, providing no evidence of measurable bias.

X Summary and Conclusions

We have presented the blind hierarchical analysis of the TDCOSMO-2026 dataset, comprising 11 lensed quasars with measured time delays. We have also considered the combination of TDCOSMO-2026 with expanded samples of non-time-delay lenses, used to constrain the internal mass-sheet parameter λint\lambda_{\rm int}. The dataset and analysis methods have substantially changed and improved with respect to our previous TDCOSMO-2025 milestone. The most important changes are: we have expanded the sample with three new systems; we have improved the kinematic data using JWST-NIRSpec spatially resolved kinematics for six out of the 11 systems; we have replaced inclination-corrected spherical models with axisymmetric ones; we have replaced estimates of the line-of-sight external convergence based on the Millennium simulations with ones based on Euclid Flagship simulations; we have used JWST-NIRCam lens models for three lenses, replacing previous ones based on HST imaging data. The main results can be summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    In flat-Λ\LambdaCDM we find H0=71.1−2.3+2.4H_{0}=71.1^{+2.4}_{-2.3} km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} for the TDCOSMO-2026 sample in our baseline model that contains solely time-delay lenses. The result is robust to variations in analysis choices and cosmological priors.

  2. 2.

    In Flat Λ\LambdaCDM we find H0=71.3−2.1+2.2H_{0}=71.3^{+2.2}_{-2.1} km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} for the TDCOSMO-2026 +SLACS+SL2S sample that also contains non-time-delay lenses.

  3. 3.

    With a 3% precision, TDCOSMO is among the most precise late-Universe probes, second only to the local distance ladder.

  4. 4.

    Our inferred H0H_{0} in flat Λ\LambdaCDM is within 1σ\sigma of measurements based on the local distance ladder [3, 1].

  5. 5.

    Our baseline H0H_{0} lies 1.6​σ1.6\sigma above the Planck value. Combining the time-delay lenses with the SLACS and SL2S samples raises this to 1.9​σ1.9\sigma with DES-Dovekie and 2.2​σ2.2\sigma with DESI-DR2 BAO, the largest difference among our Λ​CDM\mathrm{\Lambda CDM} results.

  6. 6.

    Combining TDCOSMO with other late-universe probes yields a tension with Planck at the ∼2.7​σ\sim 2.7\sigma level or more, even when excluding the local distance ladder, as discussed in our companion article (TDCOSMO-2026-PRL).

  7. 7.

    The Hubble constant is robust to the choice of background cosmology. We find H0=72.3−3.7+3.7H_{0}=72.3^{+3.7}_{-3.7} km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} in open Λ\LambdaCDM. In combination with our DES-Dovekie baseline, we find H0=71.4−2.1+2.2H_{0}=71.4^{+2.2}_{-2.1} km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} in wwCDM, H0=70.6−2.1+2.1H_{0}=70.6^{+2.1}_{-2.1} km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} in w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM, and H0=71.1−2.1+2.2H_{0}=71.1^{+2.2}_{-2.1} km​s−1​Mpc−1{\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}} in wϕw_{\phi}CDM.

  8. 8.

    Without CMB data, the combination of TDCOSMO with DESI BAO and DES-Dovekie favors a present-day equation of state w0>−1w_{0}>-1 in every extension of Λ​CDM\mathrm{\Lambda CDM} we consider: w=−0.91−0.04+0.04w=-0.91^{+0.04}_{-0.04} in wwCDM, w0=−0.85−0.06+0.07w_{0}=-0.85^{+0.07}_{-0.06} in w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM and w0=−0.88−0.05+0.04w_{0}=-0.88^{+0.04}_{-0.05} in wϕw_{\phi}CDM, disfavoring w=−1w=-1 at 2.32.3–2.5​σ2.5\sigma.

  9. 9.

    Our blind results are in excellent agreement with our previous blind determinations of the Hubble constant. This was not a foregone conclusion considering the blindness of the analysis and the many changes in the data, methods, and individual investigators involved in the analysis.

Appendix A Kinematic classification of the TDCOSMO deflectors

We classify the deflectors in the TDCOSMO sample with 2D kinematics as fast or slow rotators using the stellar spin parameter λR=∑nFn​Rn​|Vn|/∑nFn​Rn​Vrms,n\lambda_{R}=\sum_{n}F_{n}R_{n}|V_{n}|\,/\sum_{n}F_{n}R_{n}V_{\mathrm{rms},n}, with Vrms2=V2+σ2V_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}=V^{2}+\sigma^{2} [193], measured within an elliptical aperture. For B1608++656, SDSS J1206++4332 and RX J1131−-1231, we compute λR\lambda_{R} from our JWST-NIRSpec IFU kinematics, assigning each spaxel the VV and VrmsV_{\mathrm{rms}} of its bin and weighting by the flux of the deflector. Uncertainties are measured using 2000 Monte Carlo realisations drawn from the VV and VrmsV_{\mathrm{rms}} covariance matrices. For the remaining deflectors, we take λR\lambda_{R} from the corresponding papers (SDSS J1433++6007, [30]; J1537−-3010, [84]; HE 0435−-1223, PG 1115++080 and WFI 2033−-4723, [86]). The aperture used to measure λR\lambda_{R} is not uniform across the sample, because the spatial extent of the kinematic data relative to ReR_{\mathrm{e}} differs between systems.

Fig. 14 shows the deflectors in the (λR,ε)(\lambda_{R},\varepsilon) plane, together with the slow-rotator region λR<0.08+ε/4\lambda_{R}<0.08+\varepsilon/4, ε<0.4\varepsilon<0.4 [192]. For comparison, we show MAGNUS early-type galaxies [191] with σe>180\sigma_{\mathrm{e}}>180 km s-1, which span a redshift (0.24<z<0.750.24<z<0.75) and velocity dispersion range similar to those of the TDCOSMO deflectors and use the same λR\lambda_{R} definition. Atmospheric seeing smears light and biases λR\lambda_{R} low, so a PSF correction [194] is important for seeing-limited data such as MAGNUS [195]. For the JWST/NIRSpec measurements, the PSF (FWHM ∼0.15\sim 0.15 arcsec) is several times smaller than the deflector effective radii (0.530.53–1.511.51 arcsec), and we apply no correction. The values for SDSS J1433++6007 (KCWI) and J1537−-3010 (MUSE), however, come from seeing-limited data and may be biased low. Apart from B1608++656 and PG 1115++080, all deflectors lie in or at the edge of the slow-rotator region.

Appendix B Cosmographic goodness of fit

We assess how well the cosmological and population model is reproducing the measured time-delay distance of each lens by comparing the DΔ​tD_{\Delta t} measured from the lens model and time delays with the one predicted by the maximum-likelihood point of the hierarchical inference (Λ\LambdaCDM1a of Table 4). The prediction combines the cosmological distances with the population-level internal MST, λint\lambda_{\rm int}, and the external convergence of each line of sight. Its uncertainty therefore includes the intrinsic scatter σ⁡(λint)\sigma(\lambda_{\rm int}) and the uncertainty on κext\kappa_{\rm ext}, which together amount to 9–12% per lens and dominate over the 2–10% precision of most DΔ​tD_{\Delta t} measurements. Fig. 15 shows the ratio of the predicted to the measured DΔ​tD_{\Delta t}.

All eleven lenses are reproduced within 2​σ2\sigma, with χ2=10.0\chi^{2}=10.0 for 11 lenses. The largest deviations are for RX J1131−-1231, whose measured DΔ​tD_{\Delta t} lies 1.9​σ1.9\sigma below the prediction, and SDSS J1433++6007, which lies 1.6​σ1.6\sigma above it. These two systems pull the population mean of λint\lambda_{\rm int} in opposite directions: RX J1131−-1231 prefers a lower λint\lambda_{\rm int} than the sample average, as already noted in TDCOSMO-2025, while SDSS J1433++6007 prefers a higher one, in line with the individual analysis of Sheu et al. [30].

Appendix C Kinematic goodness of fit

In Figs. 16, 17 and 18, we compare the measured vrmsv_{\rm rms} with the predictions of the maximum-likelihood of the hierarchical model, for the TDCOSMO lenses (Λ\LambdaCDM1a) and for the SLACS and SL2S lenses in the joint inference (Λ\LambdaCDM4a). The model errors are split into two parts. The first is the lens-model uncertainty at fixed population parameters, shown as error bars on the model points (in blue). The second is the scatter induced by the population distributions of λint\lambda_{\rm int}, of the anisotropy and of the intrinsic axis ratio, shown as a blue band. For most lenses, the population scatter dominates the total model uncertainty. The measurement uncertainties are shown as orange error bars.

Appendix D Posterior distribution

In Table 6, we list the constraints on all the cosmological and population-level parameters sampled in the flat Λ​CDM\mathrm{\Lambda CDM} runs of Table 4. The individual power-law slopes γpl,i\gamma_{{\rm pl},i} are also sampled for each lens, but are not listed in this Table. Instead, we compare the γpl,i\gamma_{{\rm pl},i} posteriors with their lensing-only priors in Fig. 19, which also shows the shift of each posterior induced by the kinematic data, in units of the prior standard deviation. The population parameters are remarkably stable across the different lens samples and the choice of external cosmological dataset. The population means and scatters of λint\lambda_{\rm int}, σt/σr\sigma_{\rm t}/\sigma_{\rm r} and qintq_{\rm int}, as well as αλ\alpha_{\lambda}, are compatible across the different lens samples and choices of Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} prior. Most differences are within ∼1​σ\sim 1\sigma; the largest, about 1.5​σ1.5\sigma for αλ\alpha_{\lambda} and σ⁡(qint)\sigma(q_{\rm int}), arise between samples with and without the SLACS lenses.

Appendix E New unpublished spectra

Keck KCWI/KCRM IFU data for three SLACS systems (SLACJ0959+0410, SLACJ1218+0830, and SLACJ0728+3835) and one SL2S system (SL2SJ0226−-0420) were integrated within circular apertures of 1′′radius from the center of the deflector galaxy. These spectra and their best kinematic model fits with the squirrel pipeline are presented in Fig. 20. Measured kinematics and their models from the joint inference are presented in Figs. 17 and 18. Uncertainties are calculated following the methodology of Knabel et al. [69]. spatially resolved kinematics will be presented in a forthcoming paper.
